workbookTitle: Learning to Program with a Visual Novel in Scratch
welcome:
A course for everyone who loves stories (grades 5–8).

Ada Lovelace and Margaret Hamilton will guide you through this workbook. You will design your own visual novel and gradually implement it in Scratch.

Open the original German workbook PDF
variablesIntro: First, get to know variables. A variable stores a value that can change while a program is running.
listsIntro: Lists store several ordered values. Later, you will use them to build your visual novel from structured data.
chapter2GoalTitle: Chapter goal: Change scenes with the same key
chapter2Goal: Long scripts and a separate key for every scene are impractical. Use tables, lists, and a scene number so that the same key advances to the next scene.
chapter3GoalTitle: Chapter goal: Read positions from data
chapter3Goal: Extend your structured visual novel so characters can change their x and y positions on the stage.
chapter4GoalTitle: Extension: Two characters at the same time
chapter4Goal: Optional, if you have more than one lesson left: Show two characters in one scene at the same time.
appendixLanguage: Open the language menu (globe icon) in Scratch and choose your language. The illustrated original instructions are linked below.
appendixCsv:
1. Choose File in your spreadsheet application.
  2. Choose Save as and open your project folder.
  3. Select CSV UTF-8 (comma delimited) as the file type.
  4. Save the file.
appendixHints:
Hint 1: You only need one sprite. Add all actors as costumes of that sprite.

Hint 2: Try placing list items into your blocks.

task1: Use a search engine: What is a visual novel? Then name three characteristics of a visual novel.
task2: Open scratch.mit.edu and click “Create” in the top-left corner.
task3: Watch the first Scratch tutorial to get to know Scratch. If necessary, use the language instructions in the appendix.
task4: Explore Scratch. List every block category. Which categories contain “say …”, “… = …”, and “when … key pressed”? Also describe what motion blocks do to a sprite.
task5: Choose three sprites and one backdrop for your visual novel. Record sprites 1–3 and the backdrop.
task6: Draw your visual novel on white paper for 30 minutes. Use no more than eight scenes per sheet and arrange them in reading order. Record how many scenes you completed.
task8: Save the scene, rename the file Scene1_LastNameFirstName.sb3, and move it to the exchange folder.
task9: Create two more scenes that start with different keys (for example 1–3). Save the project as StructuredScenes_LastNameFirstName.sb3. Then sketch a script that plays three scenes in sequence after the green flag is clicked. What problems arise as the script grows and when there are more than 100 scenes?
task10: Create variables a (“For all sprites”) and b (“For this sprite only”). Select different sprites and describe which variables are available.
task11: Rebuild the pictured script and run it. Then replace 10 with Hello and run it again. What do you notice, especially about b? Can a variable contain text, numbers, or both at different times?
task12: Extend the script as shown, change Hello to 0, click the green flag, and press space several times. Describe what “change … by …” does.
task13: Use -1 instead of 1. Describe the difference from task 12.
task14: Use the word null instead of 0. What do you observe?
task15: Study the pictured script without rebuilding it yet. Decide whether a is repeatedly set to 11, changes by 1, causes a text error, or cannot run. Explain your choice.
task16: Rebuild the script from task 15 and check your prediction.
task17: Create a list under “Variables” and add items. Can it contain only text, only numbers, one type at a time, or text and numbers together? Justify your answer with your experiment.
task18: Right-click the list on the stage. Which options are offered?
task19: Research “import” and “export” and explain both terms in your own words.
task20: Fill the list with numbers, rebuild the pictured script, and run it. Describe what you observe.
task21: Change the value 1 in the task 20 script, test several values, and describe how the result changes.
task23: Create a spreadsheet like the example for your first three scenes and save it as a CSV file in the project folder. Does one scene correspond to a row or a column?
task24: Create one Scratch list per table column. Import the CSV data and describe how the same scene is identified across the lists.
task25: Add a variable that counts which scene is currently active.
task26: Plan how every press of the same key can construct the next scene from list items. Describe your solution and use the appendix hints if needed.
task27: Implement your plan and save the project as VisualNovel1_LastNameFirstName.sb3 in the exchange folder.
task28: Add x-position and y-position columns to the table. How are positions represented in Scratch?
task29: Add both position lists to your Scratch project.
task30: Adapt the script so sprites read their positions from the lists. Save it as VisualNovel2_LastNameFirstName.sb3.
task31: Spend 30 minutes adding more scenes to your table. Record how many scenes you completed.
task32: Compare a visual novel on paper with one in Scratch. Record advantages and disadvantages of each.
task33: Read this story: Tanja drew a 54-page visual novel. When page 20 is missing, she must redraw everything after it; Susanne recommends Scratch. Add any new ideas to your answer for task 32.
task34: Read the definition: Computer science processes, stores, and transmits information systematically and automatically. Programs contain instructions; data processing can be manual, machine-assisted, or automated and follows the input–process–output principle. Explain why your tasks were computer science and how data structuring speeds up further development of your visual novel. Compare the stages in this workbook.
task36: Create two CSV tables: table 1 contains the previous data, with one or two rows forming a scene. Table 2 contains the number of associated rows for each scene.
task37: Before creating the lists, test “broadcast …” in a stage script and “when I receive …” on a sprite. Describe how the two blocks work together.
task38: Create a list for every column in both tables.
task40: Using your previous script, create a program that shows one or two sprites in each scene. Save it as VisualNovel3_LastNameFirstName.sb3.
task41: Complete your visual novel using the two-sprite solution.
